short_description: White-domed basilica crowning the highest point of Montmartre with sweeping views over Paris.
orientation: Face south from the parvis for a panoramic view across the city rooftops.

beats.script_body: The Basilica of the Sacred Heart was built between 1875 and 1914 as a national penance after France's defeat in the Franco-Prussian War. Architect Paul Abadie designed it in a Romano-Byzantine style inspired by the Cathedral of Saint-Front in Perigueux. The travertine stone from Chateau-Landon was chosen because it secretes calcite when wet, keeping the facade perpetually white even after a century of Parisian rain and pollution.
beats.physical_cue: Look up at the gleaming white dome — the stone self-cleans with every rainfall.
beats.source_passage: Archives of the Archdiocese of Paris; Abadie architectural records.

beats.script_body: Local artists in Montmartre whisper that the basilica was built over the exact spot where Saint Denis, the first Bishop of Paris, was beheaded by Roman soldiers around 250 AD. According to legend, Denis picked up his severed head and walked ten kilometers north while preaching a sermon. The hill's name — Mons Martyrum, the Martyrs' Hill — preserves this grisly tale.
beats.physical_cue: The crypt beneath the basilica marks the legendary site of Denis's martyrdom.
beats.source_passage: Gregory of Tours, History of the Franks; Montmartre parish records.

short_description: Neoclassical mausoleum in the Latin Quarter honoring France's greatest citizens.
orientation: Stand in the nave beneath the dome where Foucault's pendulum once demonstrated the Earth's rotation.

beats.script_body: Mirabeau was the first person interred in the Pantheon after the National Assembly repurposed it as a secular temple during the Revolution in 1791. But his body was removed just two years later when his secret correspondence with Louis XVI was discovered. The Pantheon has always been political — bodies are moved in and out depending on who holds power. Voltaire and Rousseau were placed here as symbols of Enlightenment triumph over monarchy. Victor Hugo's funeral in 1885 drew two million mourners through the streets of Paris, the largest public gathering the city had ever seen. The building's inscription — Aux grands hommes, la patrie reconnaissante — was itself contested, since no woman was admitted until Marie Curie in 1995, two centuries after it opened.
beats.physical_cue: The inscription above the portico reads 'Aux grands hommes, la patrie reconnaissante.'
beats.source_passage: Archives nationales de France; Pantheon administrative records.

beats.script_body: The Pantheon's architecture tells a story of competing visions. Louis XV commissioned Jacques-Germain Soufflot in 1758 to build a church dedicated to Sainte Genevieve, the patron saint of Paris. Soufflot envisioned a fusion of Gothic structural lightness with classical grandeur — a daring experiment that nearly killed the project. The massive dome, inspired by St. Peter's in Rome and St. Paul's in London, required innovative iron reinforcements that were controversial among his peers. Soufflot died in 1780 before completion, and his student Jean-Baptiste Rondelet finished the work. During the Revolution, Quatremere de Quincy sealed the lower windows to create the somber, tomb-like atmosphere that persists today. The original church was flooded with natural light — a vision now lost beneath layers of revolutionary ideology.
beats.physical_cue: Look up at the dome — the sealed lower windows are visible from inside as blank stone panels.
beats.source_passage: Soufflot architectural drawings; Bibliotheque nationale de France.

orientation: Look for the wooden carriage door between the two stone buildings on Rue de Furstemberg.

beats.script_body: A tiny garden hides behind the apartment facades. Locals call it the secret square.

poi_name: UI Test — Tower of London Gate
short_description: The ancient royal fortress on the Thames — far outside Paris's geofence.
orientation: Face the main entrance on Tower Hill approaching from the Underground station.

beats.script_body: The Tower of London was founded by William the Conqueror in 1066 as a symbol of Norman power over the conquered Anglo-Saxons. The White Tower at its center was the tallest building in London for centuries. It has served as a royal palace, prison, armory, treasury, and menagerie — at one point housing lions, an elephant, and a polar bear that fished in the Thames on a long chain.
beats.physical_cue: The White Tower stands at the center of the complex, its pale Caen stone still visible.
beats.source_passage: Historic Royal Palaces archives; Tower of London records.

short_description: First of two entries sharing a name — tests duplicate resolver.
orientation: Start at the riverside near the Pont Neuf.

beats.script_body: The banks of the Seine were classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1991, recognizing the river's role as the spine of Paris for over two thousand years. The quays were built progressively from the 16th to 19th centuries, transforming muddy flood-prone banks into the elegant stone promenades we walk today. The bouquinistes — second-hand booksellers whose green stalls line the parapets — have been here since the 16th century and are considered the world's largest open-air bookshop.
beats.physical_cue: Green wooden bookstall boxes line the stone parapet along the river.
beats.source_passage: UNESCO World Heritage nomination dossier; Paris municipal archives.

short_description: Second of two entries sharing a name — tests duplicate resolver.
orientation: Continue east along the left bank past the Pont de la Tournelle toward Notre-Dame.

beats.script_body: The eastern stretch of the Seine promenade passes beneath Notre-Dame where you can see the flying buttresses from below. At sunset the limestone facades of the Ile Saint-Louis turn golden and the cathedral's silhouette darkens against the sky like a paper cutout. Barges glide past carrying tourists who crane their necks upward at the same view that Impressionist painters captured a century ago.
beats.physical_cue: The flying buttresses of Notre-Dame are visible above the tree line from the left bank.
beats.source_passage: Paris riverfront walking guide; Ile Saint-Louis historical society.

short_description: Historic marketplace testing multi-lens beat rendering and editing.
orientation: Enter the Canopee from Rue Rambuteau facing the curved glass roof.

beats.script_body: Les Halles served as the central food market of Paris for over eight centuries, from the reign of Louis VI in 1137 until its demolition in 1971. The iron-and-glass pavilions designed by Victor Baltard in the 1850s were engineering marvels — twelve vast halls inspired by railway station architecture, each devoted to a different category of food. Emile Zola called Les Halles 'the belly of Paris' in his 1873 novel. The demolition to make way for a shopping center remains one of the most controversial urban planning decisions in French history.
beats.physical_cue: The modern Canopee roof echoes the curved lines of Baltard's vanished iron pavilions.
beats.source_passage: Baltard architectural records; Archives de Paris; Zola, Le Ventre de Paris.

beats.script_body: Beneath the modern Forum des Halles lies an older Paris. Workers digging the underground shopping complex in the 1970s uncovered medieval cellars and ossuary passages connected to the nearby Cimetiere des Innocents, which had been the city's main burial ground for six centuries before its closure in 1786. Bones were transferred to the Catacombs, but rumors persist that some passages remain sealed and unexplored.
beats.physical_cue: A sealed stone archway near the lower parking levels marks one rumored passage entrance.
beats.source_passage: Paris underground survey; Cimetiere des Innocents excavation reports.

beats.script_body: The food stalls of the original Les Halles operated through the night, feeding a city that never truly slept. Porters, butchers, and fishmongers worked from midnight to dawn. After the market closed, the tradition survived in the surrounding bistros that still serve French onion soup — soupe a l'oignon gratinee — in the early morning hours, a dish born from the need to feed exhausted market workers cheaply and quickly.
beats.physical_cue: The narrow streets around Rue Montorgueil still host food vendors continuing the market tradition.
beats.source_passage: Paris culinary history archives; Rue Montorgueil merchant records.

beats.script_body: Street musicians at Les Halles carry on a tradition stretching back to medieval jongleurs who performed for market crowds. The underground corridors of the Forum des Halles and the adjacent RER station Chatelet-Les Halles have become one of Paris's most vibrant stages for buskers, with the city issuing official permits to performers since 1997.
beats.physical_cue: The underground corridors between the RER platforms where musicians set up with amplifiers.
beats.source_passage: Paris busking history; RATP performance permit archives.

poi_name: UI Test — The Extraordinarily Long-Named Historical Marker at the Corner of Boulevard Saint-Germain and Rue de l'Ancienne-Comedie
short_description: This is a deliberately long description designed to test how the workbench handles text overflow in the worklist row and detail view. It describes a historical marker at the intersection of Boulevard Saint-Germain and Rue de l'Ancienne-Comedie in the sixth arrondissement of Paris where the first permanent public coffeehouse in France, Le Procope, opened in 1686. The cafe became a gathering place for Enlightenment philosophers including Voltaire, Rousseau, and Diderot, and later served as a meeting point for revolutionary leaders Danton, Marat, and Robespierre. The commemorative plaque was installed in 1986 during the tricentennial celebrations of the cafe's founding.
orientation: Stand at the northwest corner of the intersection facing the stone building with the commemorative bronze plaque mounted approximately two meters above street level on the facade between the ground floor windows and the first floor balcony. You may need to look carefully as the plaque has weathered significantly since its installation during the 1986 tricentennial celebrations of Le Procope.

beats.script_body: Le Procope, opened in 1686 by Sicilian Francesco Procopio dei Coltelli, was the first coffeehouse in Paris and became the intellectual nerve center of the Enlightenment. Voltaire allegedly drank forty cups of coffee a day here while writing. During the Revolution, Danton and Marat plotted in its back rooms while Napoleon left his hat as collateral when he couldn't pay his bill — it hung on the wall for years.
beats.physical_cue: The bronze plaque on the stone facade between the ground floor and first floor balcony.
beats.source_passage: Le Procope historical archives; Paris cafe culture records.

short_description: Conflict test POI — same GPS as the seeded 'Champ de Mars Landmark' but a different name, so it surfaces a proximity match to resolve.
orientation: Face the tower from the Champ de Mars looking northwest.

beats.script_body: Gustave Eiffel's iron tower was never meant to last. Built as a temporary entrance arch for the 1889 World's Fair celebrating the centennial of the French Revolution, the 300-meter tower was scheduled for demolition after twenty years. Eiffel saved it by installing a radio transmitter at its summit, making it indispensable for military communications. During World War I it intercepted a coded German message that led to the arrest of spy Mata Hari.
beats.physical_cue: The iron lattice tower rising above the Champ de Mars.
beats.source_passage: Eiffel company archives; 1889 World's Fair records.

beats.script_body: Jazz clubs once lined the streets around the Champ de Mars drawing musicians from New Orleans and Harlem. After World War I, Black American musicians found a freedom in Paris that Jim Crow denied them at home. Sidney Bechet, Josephine Baker, and Django Reinhardt turned Montparnasse and Saint-Germain into the jazz capital of Europe. Smoky basement clubs along Rue de Rennes hosted late night jam sessions where unknown artists sat in with legends.
beats.physical_cue: The narrow side streets off Avenue de la Bourdonnais where basement club entrances still have their iron railings.
beats.source_passage: Paris jazz history oral archives; Josephine Baker biography.

beats.script_body: Gustave Eiffel himself maintained a private apartment at the summit of the tower where he entertained distinguished guests including Thomas Edison. The apartment was furnished with velvet settees, a grand piano, and scientific instruments. Parisians who had mocked the tower as a metal monstrosity begged for invitations. Eiffel refused nearly all of them, preferring to use the space for meteorological and aerodynamic experiments that contributed to early aviation research.
beats.physical_cue: The small windows at the very top of the tower mark Eiffel's private apartment.
beats.source_passage: Eiffel personal papers; Societe des Ingenieurs Civils de France.

beats.script_body: When the tower was first unveiled, Parisian artists erupted in fury. A petition signed by Guy de Maupassant, Alexandre Dumas fils, and Charles Garnier called it a disgrace — a factory chimney disfiguring the city's skyline. Maupassant famously ate lunch at the tower's restaurant every day, claiming it was the only place in Paris where he didn't have to look at it. Street artists responded by sketching the tower obsessively, turning protest into a new visual vocabulary that influenced Art Nouveau.
beats.physical_cue: The esplanade beneath the tower where caricaturists still sketch visitors, continuing a tradition from opening day.
beats.source_passage: 1887 Artists' Petition; Paris art history archives.

beats.script_body: The Champ de Mars beneath the tower was originally a military drill ground — its name means Field of Mars, the Roman god of war. Before that, the site was farmland and vineyards. Today the long rectangular garden stretching from the tower to the Ecole Militaire supports over 80 species of trees and provides nesting habitat for kestrels, which hunt pigeons from the tower's upper platforms. The falcons have become so established that ornithologists study them as an example of urban raptor adaptation.
beats.physical_cue: The rows of chestnut and plane trees lining the Champ de Mars beneath the tower.
beats.source_passage: Paris urban ecology survey; Museum national d'Histoire naturelle raptor studies.

beats.script_body: Montmartre's winding lanes and steep staircases make it one of the most painted neighborhoods in the world. The violet-tinged windowpanes on several Rue Lepic buildings are the result of manganese dioxide in 19th-century glass reacting with decades of sunlight — they were never intentionally tinted. Renoir, Toulouse-Lautrec, and later Picasso worked within steps of these windows.
beats.physical_cue: Look for the violet-tinged windowpanes on the upper floors along Rue Lepic.
beats.source_passage: Montmartre architectural survey; 19th-century glass chemistry records.

audit_notes.issue: Violet windowpane claim needs primary source verification.
audit_notes.suggested_fix: Add citation to the manganese dioxide chemical analysis from 1990s restoration reports.

beats.script_body: The Bateau-Lavoir studio on Rue Ravignan is where Pablo Picasso painted Les Demoiselles d'Avignon in 1907, the work that shattered Western art's perspective conventions and launched Cubism. The building was a ramshackle former piano factory with no heating and a single water tap. Picasso, Juan Gris, Amedeo Modigliani, and Kees van Dongen worked here in freezing conditions, burning their drawings for warmth. The original building was destroyed by fire in 1970 and rebuilt.
beats.physical_cue: The reconstructed facade of the Bateau-Lavoir at 13 Rue Ravignan.
beats.source_passage: Musee de Montmartre archives; Picasso biographical records.

audit_notes.issue: Date verification needed — some sources say the painting was started in late 1906.
audit_notes.suggested_fix: Clarify: 'began in late 1906 and completed in July 1907.'
audit_notes.source: Museum of Modern Art curatorial notes.
